clue.text: Main sort of afflictions Hamlet might oppose ?

definitions.text: Main sort of afflictions Hamlet might oppose ?

parts.words: Main sort of afflictions Hamlet might oppose ?
parts.note: Hamlet speaks of taking arms against a sea of woes; 'main' is an old word for the sea, so the clue asks for the woes that come in a sea

explanation.surface: A question about what sort of hardships the Prince of Denmark would fight against.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Main' looks like 'chief' but is the poetic word for the ocean, pointing to the line 'to take arms against a sea of ...' from Hamlet's 'To be or not to be' speech.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means difficulties or woes, and it completes Shakespeare's phrase about a sea of them.

clue.text: Put up suitable bit of fish for lunch

indicators.note: in a down clue, putting a word up means writing it from bottom to top

parts.note: fit means suitable
a fin is a part of a fish

explanation.surface: Serve a proper piece of fish as the midday meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put up' turns FIT to TIF, followed by FIN. Tiffin is the Anglo-Indian word for a light midday meal.
explanation.definitionFit: An Anglo-Indian term for a light midday meal.

clue.text: We might see scores of such entertainments

definitions.text: We might see scores of such entertainments

parts.words: We might see scores of such entertainments
parts.note: 'scores' reads as dozens, but means written music, which these staged musical dramas use

explanation.surface: We could attend many such shows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scores' suggests large numbers; it is the music written out for a staged sung drama.
explanation.definitionFit: Staged dramas sung to orchestral music, each written in a score.

clue.text: Music played on board?

explanation.surface: Tunes performed aboard ship.
explanation.definitionFit: A short light piece for piano is so called; and it is also a game in which balls are struck along a table into holes.

clue.text: Cites Hunt as one sort that's zealous

indicators.note: to sort is to rearrange into order, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Someone names a man called Hunt as a keen type of person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sort' looks like a noun, a kind, but it is the anagram signal: CITES HUNT AS plus I make twelve letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe eager, keen devotion to a cause.

clue.text: Gem returned by local a airman? 16

annotationWithheld.why: Gem returned by local airmen? (6): SCARAB reversed is BARACS, and no reading found makes 'local airmen' give those letters
annotationWithheld.clue: Gem returned by local a airman? 16

clue.text: With an emperor he heard the voice of Keats's nightingale

definitions.text: With an emperor he heard the voice of Keats's nightingale

parts.words: With an emperor he heard the voice of Keats's nightingale
parts.note: Keats's Ode to a Nightingale says the bird's voice 'was heard / In ancient days by emperor and' a jester-like figure

explanation.surface: A literary quiz about who listened to Keats's songbird alongside a ruler.
explanation.walkthrough: The line from the Ode is 'The voice I hear this passing night was heard / In ancient days by emperor and ...'.
explanation.definitionFit: A buffoon or fool, the humble counterpart Keats pairs with the ruler.

clue.text: Trust new cleaner to come about one

indicators.note: the rearranged letters come around, or enclose, the letter for one
new signals that the letters of cleaner are made into a fresh arrangement

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Faith that a newly hired cleaner will arrive at one o'clock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New' rearranges CLEANER to RELANCE, and 'to come about' puts I inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words mean dependence or confidence placed in someone.

clue.text: Fragile little water-casks?

parts.note: small kegs for drinking water on a ship are called by a name that also suggests things that break easily

explanation.surface: Small barrels for water that are easily broken.
explanation.walkthrough: A breaker is a small water keg kept in a ship's boat; the question mark asks whether such casks are fragile because of their name.
explanation.definitionFit: Small kegs carried in boats for fresh water bear this name, which also sounds like things that shatter.

clue.text: Cargoes for French crews

parts.note: an eight is a rowing crew of eight oarsmen, so crews are eights

explanation.surface: Shipments destined for the crews of French vessels.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crews' suggests sailors, but here it means rowing eights.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words name goods carried by ship, lorry or train.

clue.text: Dog the miner docked

indicators.note: docked, like a dog's tail, means cut short, so the last letter is removed

parts.note: a collier is a coal miner

explanation.surface: An order to follow the coal miner whose pay has been cut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Docked' takes the final R off COLLIER. 'Dog' looks like a verb, to follow, but it is the definition: a sheepdog breed.
explanation.definitionFit: A Border or rough collie is a breed of sheepdog.

clue.text: Correct speech still in one Cambridge college ?

explanation.surface: Proper diction is still spoken at a Cambridge college.
explanation.walkthrough: King's is a Cambridge college, so its English is the language as still found in King's.
explanation.definitionFit: Standard educated usage is named after the monarch; and the subject English taught at the royal college at Cambridge.

clue.text: Until pianist is left out — gets upset

indicators.note: upset means overturned or disturbed, so the remaining letters are rearranged
the word 'is' is to be removed from the letters of pianist

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A pianist who is unsuited to the job is dropped and takes it badly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left out' removes I and S from PIANIST, leaving PIANT; 'gets upset' rearranges those letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words mean unsuitable or not appropriate for a purpose.

clue.text: Trade combine has means of raising the standard

parts.note: a trade union is a combination of workers in a trade
a jack is a device for lifting a car or heavy load

explanation.surface: A trade union owns equipment for hoisting the flag.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Raising the standard' reads as raising the flag or raising quality; the standard is the definition, Britain's national flag.
explanation.definitionFit: A standard is a flag, and this is the national flag of the United Kingdom.

clue.text: Ugly fires can wreck a space ship

indicators.note: to wreck is to smash up, so the letters of the three words before are broken and rebuilt

explanation.surface: Dreadful blazes might destroy a rocket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Can' looks like a verb but its letters are part of the fodder: UGLY FIRES CAN, twelve letters, rearranged by 'wreck'.
explanation.definitionFit: A disc-shaped craft supposedly carrying visitors from other worlds is a kind of spacecraft.

clue.text: Even appears quite old-fashioned

parts.note: all means quite or completely, as in 'all alone'
square is slang for conventional or out of date

explanation.surface: Even so, it looks rather dated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Appears' is a link word. The answer is the sporting term for scores being level.
explanation.definitionFit: Level scores, with neither side ahead, as in golf or a debt settled.

clue.text: The herald's lying!

parts.note: not a herald telling lies: the heraldic term for a beast shown lying down with its head raised

explanation.surface: An accusation that the royal messenger is not telling the truth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lying' suggests deceit; in heraldry it describes a beast lying down, a term heralds use.
explanation.definitionFit: A heraldic term for an animal shown resting with its head raised.

clue.text: Star is given broken seat — some chance of injury

indicators.note: broken signals that the letters of seat are smashed and reassembled

parts.note: risk is a chance of harm or injury

explanation.surface: A celebrity given a broken chair faces a danger of getting hurt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Star' is not a celebrity but the printed star symbol. 'Broken' turns SEAT into ASTE.
explanation.definitionFit: The typographic mark * is named for its star shape.

clue.text: Cases of natives being seen on board, perhaps

definitions.text: Cases of natives being seen on board, perhaps

parts.words: Cases of natives being seen on board, perhaps
parts.note: 'natives' are oysters raised in British waters, and their cases are the hard coverings, seen on a serving board or a ship's board

explanation.surface: Suitcases belonging to local people are spotted aboard a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Natives' is the trade name for British-bred oysters, especially from Whitstable; 'cases' are their protective coverings, not luggage.
explanation.definitionFit: The hard bivalve casings of edible molluscs, as left on a platter.

clue.text: Oil producer with striking clothes ?

parts.note: a rig is a drilling installation that produces oil
workers who are striking are out

explanation.surface: An oil company with workers on strike asks about outfits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Striking' looks like 'eye-catching' but means on strike, OUT.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for an outfit, especially a showy one.

clue.text: Behind some of Pasternak's activities ?

indicators.note: only some of the letters of the phrase are used, a run inside it

explanation.surface: A question about what lies behind the Russian novelist's doings.
explanation.walkthrough: Pasternak was the Russian author of Doctor Zhivago.
explanation.definitionFit: A nautical word meaning at or towards the rear of a ship.

clue.text: Preparing the hands for striking?

parts.note: readying the hands to strike means closing them tightly into fists, not readying clock hands to strike the hour

explanation.surface: Setting a clock's hands so that it will chime.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a clock being set to strike; the answer is curling fingers into fists before a punch.
explanation.definitionFit: Tightening the fingers into a fist is what a boxer does before a blow.

clue.text: Rule found in the chapter

explanation.surface: A regulation discovered within a book section.
explanation.definitionFit: A church law or principle; and a clergyman belonging to a cathedral's governing body.

clue.text: Leaves 15?

explanation.surface: Foliage numbering fifteen.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who departs a job resigns from it; and two parties who are level or even with nothing owed are said to be square.

clue.text: People round one in a quarter of a French city

indicators.note: the built-up group is placed inside the outer letters

parts.note: taken as written
S, south, is one of the four quarters of the compass

indicators.note: the word for people goes round the letter for one

parts.note: men means people
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Locals gather round someone in one district of a city in France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Round' puts I inside MEN to make MIEN, and 'in' places that between A and S.
explanation.definitionFit: A cathedral city in Picardy, northern France.

clue.text: Opera in F ? Could be a light one

definitions.text: Opera in F ? Could be a light one

parts.words: Opera in F ? Could be a light one
parts.note: the clue points to a Gilbert and Sullivan light opera whose title, H.M.S. ..., holds the run 'in a F'; it is also the name of a light apron-dress

explanation.surface: A question about the key of an opera, answered that it may be a light opera.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Light' works twice: a comic opera is a light opera, and the title is also a light sleeveless dress or apron.
explanation.definitionFit: H.M.S. ... is a comic operetta by Gilbert and Sullivan from 1878.

clue.text: Attractive but acquisitive?

explanation.surface: Someone appealing but grasping.
explanation.definitionFit: A winning manner is called appealing; and someone grabbing things for themselves is grasping.

clue.text: Menace for variety-theatre direction

indicators.note: variety means a mixed assortment, so the letters of theatre are mixed up

parts.note: N, north, is a compass direction

explanation.surface: A danger posed to the management of music halls.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Variety' looks like part of 'variety theatre', a music hall, but it signals an anagram of THEATRE, to which N is added.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words mean to hold out the prospect of harm.
